14320:
Succinct means expressing something fully and clearly, but using as few words as possible. When something is succinct, it covers everything that needs to be said — no more, no less. Nothing important is left out, and nothing unnecessary is added.

Think of it this way: imagine you could squeeze all the meaning out of a long paragraph and pack it tightly into two sharp sentences, without losing any of the important ideas. The result would be succinct.

Here is what most people get wrong about this word: succinct does not simply mean short. A one-word answer can be short but completely useless. Succinct means short and effective and complete. It is brevity with purpose. The shortness serves the clarity, not the other way around.

A 10-page essay can be succinct if the topic genuinely needed 10 pages and there is no unnecessary filler. A two-sentence answer can be not succinct if those two sentences are vague and confused. The real measure is: does every word earn its place?

The word is used to describe things involving language and communication. You can say:

A succinct explanation — one that teaches you something clearly without burying you in unnecessary detail.

A succinct answer — one that gets straight to the point and covers what was asked without wandering off.

A succinct summary — one that captures the key points of something longer, cleanly and efficiently.

A succinct speaker or writer — a person who communicates this way habitually; someone who never wastes words.

A succinct email, message, or report — a piece of writing that respects the reader's time by being tight and focused.

Succinct is almost always a compliment. When someone calls your writing or speech succinct, they are praising you. It signals intelligence and skill, because being succinct is actually hard. Most people — when nervous, unsure, or trying too hard — add more words than necessary. Being succinct means you understood something well enough to strip it to its cleanest form.
How Succinct Differs From Similar Words

Several words are close to succinct in meaning, but each has a slightly different flavor, and knowing the differences will make you a more precise thinker.

Brief simply means short in duration or length. A brief speech is a short speech — but it might still be rambling and unclear. Brief says nothing about quality. Succinct does.

Concise is the closest synonym to succinct and is nearly interchangeable in most situations. Both mean short and effective. If there is a subtle difference, concise tends to emphasize cutting out excess, while succinct tends to emphasize the tightness and clarity of the final result. In practice, most native speakers treat them as the same.

Terse means very few words — but it can carry a slightly cold or even rude tone. A terse reply can feel like the speaker didn't want to bother with you. Succinct never has that coldness; it is neutral to positive.

Pithy means brief, but with an extra quality: a pithy remark is not only short and clear, it is also sharp, clever, or memorable — almost like a punch. "The early bird catches the worm" is pithy. Succinct doesn't require that extra punch of wit.

Laconic means using extremely few words, sometimes to an almost unusual degree. It often describes a personality type — the strong, silent person who says little. It can feel slightly aloof or mysterious. Succinct is simply about quality of communication, not personality.

The antonyms of succinct are words like verbose, wordy, long-winded, rambling, and prolix. These all describe communication that uses far more words than necessary. Verbose writing circles around its point without landing on it. Long-winded speech exhausts the listener before the point arrives. These are the enemies of succinct communication.
A Simple Test to Remember It

Whenever you read or hear something and think "they said exactly what needed to be said, nothing more and nothing less" — that thing is succinct. Whenever you read something and think "I could have said this in half the words" or "I had to dig through a lot of noise to find the point" — that thing is the opposite of succinct.

There is a quiet irony worth noticing: a truly succinct explanation of the word "succinct" would be something like — "brief, clear, and complete." But you are a learner, and a genuinely helpful explanation cannot itself be succinct, because you need the context, the comparisons, and the examples to fully understand it. Once you have read and absorbed all of the above, you will not need them anymore. At that point, "brief, clear, and complete" will be enough — and you will understand exactly why.
14321: Succor means help, relief, or support given to someone who is suffering, in serious trouble, or in urgent need. But a bare definition like that doesn't do the word justice, so let's unpack it properly.
The most important thing to understand about succor

Succor is not just any help. If you help a friend carry groceries or show a coworker how to use a new app, you wouldn't call that succor. Succor is reserved for situations where someone is genuinely suffering or in serious difficulty — and another person steps in to relieve that suffering in a meaningful way. The presence of real distress or hardship is what defines succor. Without it, the word doesn't apply.

Think of it this way: a refugee fleeing a war zone is given food, shelter, and safety — that is succor. A soldier wounded on a battlefield receives urgent medical care — that is succor. A person broken by grief finds deep comfort in the words of a trusted friend — that, too, is succor. The scale doesn't matter. What matters is that someone was truly struggling, and real, compassionate help arrived.

Succor takes many forms depending on what the suffering person needs most. It can be physical — food, water, medicine, shelter, money. It can be emotional — comfort, reassurance, companionship during grief or fear. It can even be spiritual — a sense of hope or peace given to someone in despair. The word stretches across all of these. What ties them together is not the type of help, but the fact that it was given to someone who desperately needed it.
The tone and weight of the word

Succor is a formal, serious, and somewhat literary word. You won't hear it in casual everyday conversation. It tends to appear in writing — literature, journalism, historical accounts, religious texts, and formal speeches. When a writer uses "succor," they are deliberately signalling that the help being described carries emotional and moral weight. It's a word that makes you feel the gravity of the situation and the generosity of the person giving the help. Choosing this word over "help" or "assistance" is a deliberate stylistic choice that says: this moment matters.

It helps to know the edges of the word. Succor is not routine or trivial assistance. It is not a quick favour. It is not polite but hollow comfort (saying "you'll be fine" and walking away is not succor). It is also not a transaction — succor is given out of compassion, not because something is owed or expected in return. The element of genuine care and urgency is always present.
How it sits among its synonyms

Words like aid, assistance, relief, comfort, and solace are in the same neighbourhood as succor, but none of them is a perfect match.

Aid and assistance are broader and more neutral — they can describe help in any context, urgent or not. Relief focuses specifically on easing pain or removing a burden, but doesn't always imply active, compassionate giving. Comfort and solace are more emotional and don't necessarily include physical help. Succor is unique because it brings together urgency, real distress, and compassionate action — often blending physical and emotional help at once. It carries a warmth and nobility that the other words don't always have.

"The charity provided succor to thousands of earthquake victims, distributing food, clean water, and medical supplies."

"In her darkest hour, she found succor in the quiet, steady presence of her oldest friend."

"The Red Cross has, for over a century, brought succor to people caught in the middle of war and disaster."

"He sought succor from his faith during the most painful chapter of his life."

"The villagers opened their homes to the wounded, offering succor to people they had never met."

In every case, notice the pattern: someone is in real distress, and the help they receive is meaningful, compassionate, and genuinely needed.
Succor is the compassionate help, relief, or support given to someone who is suffering or in serious need — not a casual favour, but real aid that reaches a person at a moment of genuine hardship.
14322:
To succor someone means to go to their aid and give them help, relief, or comfort when they are suffering, in danger, or in serious distress.

It is not just any kind of help. It is specifically the kind of help you give to someone who truly needs it — someone who is wounded, hungry, grief-stricken, trapped, sick, or in crisis. Think of it as rushing to someone's rescue at their lowest moment, and giving them what they urgently need to survive, recover, or feel less alone in their suffering.
What Makes It Different From Just "Help"

This is the most important thing to understand about this word, so pay close attention.

The word "help" is broad and neutral. You can help someone move a sofa, help someone with their homework, or help someone find their glasses. None of those situations involve real suffering.

Succor always involves suffering. The person being succored is in genuine need — physical, emotional, or material. And the person doing the succoring is responding to that suffering with care, compassion, and meaningful action.

So the word carries two things at once:

  • A practical action (giving food, shelter, medical care, rescue, support)
  • A human impulse behind it (empathy, duty, compassion)

When you succor someone, you don't just toss them a coin and walk away. You actually show up for them in a moment when they have no one and nothing else to lean on.
A Simple Way to Picture It

Imagine a battlefield. Soldiers are wounded. A medic runs through gunfire to reach them, dresses their wounds, and carries them to safety. That medic is succoring the wounded.

Or imagine a blizzard. A traveler is lost, freezing, and nearly unconscious. A stranger opens their home, brings the traveler inside, wraps them in blankets, and gives them hot food. That stranger is succoring the traveler.

Or imagine a refugee camp. Aid workers bring medicine, clean water, and food to thousands of displaced families who have lost everything. Those workers are succoring the refugees.

In every case, notice the pattern:

  • Someone is suffering or in desperate need
  • Someone else steps in with real, meaningful help
  • The help addresses the suffering directly
The Range of Who (or What) Can Be Succored

The verb is flexible. Here is who or what can be the object of "succor":

People — the sick, the hungry, the poor, the wounded, the grieving, the oppressed, prisoners, refugees, disaster survivors, orphans, the homeless.

Groups or communities — a struggling nation, a community hit by a hurricane, a people under siege.

Abstract things (in literary use) — a failing cause, a weakened institution, a fragile spirit.

You would NOT use succor for small, trivial situations. You would not say "she succored him by telling him where the bathroom was." That would be absurd. The word demands weight and genuine need.

• "Doctors flew into the war zone to succor the civilians caught in the crossfire."
  • "She spent thirty years succoring the poor in the slums of the city."
  • "The church opened its doors to succor the homeless during the brutal winter storm."
  • "No one came to succor the prisoners; they were left to suffer alone."
  • "Relief organizations succored thousands of families after the earthquake destroyed the town."
  • "He had been abandoned in his illness, with no one to succor him."
  • "The nation turned to its allies, hoping they would succor it in its hour of need."
The Tone and Register of This Word

"Succor" is a formal, literary word. You will rarely hear it in casual conversation. Instead, you will find it in:

  • Literature and classic novels
  • Historical writing
  • Religious texts
  • Journalism about wars, famines, and humanitarian crises
  • Formal speeches and official reports

In everyday speech, people simply say "help," "aid," or "support" instead. But those words feel thin compared to succor. When a writer chooses "succor," they are being deliberate — they want you to feel the gravity of the situation, the depth of the suffering, and the nobility of the response.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Help — general and everyday. No emotional weight. Succor is far more specific and serious.

Aid — more formal than "help," and closer to succor. But "aid" often sounds logistical (financial aid, foreign aid). Succor sounds more personal and compassionate.

Rescue — implies saving someone from immediate, acute danger. Succor is broader — it includes ongoing care and comfort, not just a single dramatic act.

Comfort — focuses on the emotional side (soothing, reassuring). Succor includes comfort but also practical help.

Relieve — to reduce someone's pain or burden. Closer to succor, but more clinical and impersonal. Succor has a warmer, more human quality.

Think of it this way: succor sits at the intersection of "aid" and "comfort." It is helping someone in a way that is both practical and deeply human.

One final thing worth understanding: succoring someone is almost always seen as a morally good and noble act. It is the kind of thing heroes, saints, caregivers, and compassionate people do. The word naturally implies that the person doing the succoring is responding to a moral call — a duty to relieve suffering when they see it.

Conversely, failing to succor someone who needs it is often implied as a failure of character or duty. In many historical and literary contexts, you will find writers condemning those who "refused to succor" the needy or the suffering — because the expectation is that decent people should.
To succor is to give urgent, compassionate help — whether physical, material, or emotional — to someone who is in genuine distress, suffering, or crisis, when they have nowhere else to turn.
14323: Succulent means full of juice, richness, and satisfying goodness. It is always a positive word — it never describes something bad or unpleasant. When you call something succulent, you are saying it is not just good, but pleasurably, almost irresistibly good.

This is the most common way the word is used.

When food is succulent, it means it is:

  • Juicy — full of natural moisture and liquid
  • Tender — soft and easy to bite into
  • Flavorful — rich in taste, not bland or dry

Think about biting into a perfectly cooked piece of chicken. The juice runs out, the meat is soft, and the flavor is deep and satisfying. That is succulent food.

Now imagine the opposite — dry, tough, flavorless chicken. That is the complete opposite of succulent.

Examples:

  • "The chef prepared a succulent lamb roast."
  • "She bit into a succulent, ripe mango."
  • "The prawns were succulent and perfectly seasoned."

What makes "succulent" special compared to just saying "juicy"?
"Juicy" simply means liquid is present. "Succulent" goes further — it suggests that the food is richly satisfying as a whole, combining juiciness, tenderness, and good flavor together. It is a fuller, more indulgent compliment. A menu using the word "succulent" is trying to make your mouth water.

The word has a well-established second meaning in the world of plants.

A succulent plant is one that has thick, fleshy, swollen leaves or stems that store water inside them. This adaptation allows the plant to survive in hot, dry environments like deserts, where rainfall is rare.

The logic connects directly to Meaning 1 — just as succulent food is full of moisture and richness, a succulent plant is literally full of stored water, making its parts thick and almost "juicy-looking."

Famous examples of succulent plants:

  • Aloe vera — the gel-filled plant used in skincare
  • Cactus — spiky desert plants with water-storing stems
  • Jade plant — a popular houseplant with thick, glossy leaves
  • Echeveria — a rosette-shaped plant commonly kept indoors

Succulent plants are extremely popular as houseplants because they require very little watering and are hard to kill.

Examples of the word used this way:

  • "Her windowsill was lined with small succulents." (Here, "succulents" is used as a noun, but the root meaning is the same adjective.)
  • "The garden featured a beautiful display of succulent plants."
Meaning 3: Describing Something Richly Appealing (Figurative Use)

Less commonly, writers and speakers use "succulent" in a figurative way to describe something that is richly attractive, tempting, or deeply interesting — not food or plants, but ideas, opportunities, or details.

Examples:

  • "The journalist uncovered some succulent details about the scandal." (Meaning: rich, juicy, fascinating details)
  • "It was a succulent business opportunity — too good to pass up." (Meaning: rich, highly attractive)

This figurative use borrows the sense of "richly satisfying goodness" from the food meaning and applies it to non-physical things. You will encounter this mostly in writing, not everyday conversation.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Succulent" is a sensory word — it paints a vivid picture and almost makes you feel something. It's slightly more formal and expressive than plain words like "juicy" or "moist." You'll often see it in:

  • Restaurant menus and food writing
  • Recipe descriptions
  • Gardening and nature writing
  • Literary or journalistic prose

It is never a negative word. You would never use it to describe something bad. If someone calls your cooking "succulent," take it as a high compliment.

ContextWhat "succulent" means
FoodJuicy, tender, rich, and deeply flavorful
PlantsHaving thick, fleshy parts that store water
FigurativeRichly attractive, tempting, or fascinatingly detailed

In one sentence: Succulent describes something that is richly full of moisture, flavor, or goodness — whether it's a piece of meat, a desert plant, or even an irresistible opportunity.
14324:
Imagine you are in a tug-of-war. You are pulling as hard as you can, trying not to lose. But the force on the other side is stronger than you. Slowly, your grip weakens. Your feet start sliding. And finally — you let go. You couldn't hold on anymore.

That moment of giving in — that is succumbing.

"Succumb" means to stop resisting something that is stronger than you, and give in to it — usually because you have no choice, or because the force is simply too powerful to fight off any longer.

The word almost always implies that a struggle happened first. The person or thing was holding on, resisting, fighting — and then couldn't anymore.

1. To give in to a force, pressure, temptation, or influence

This is the most common use. Someone is trying to resist something — and eventually, that something wins.

Examples:

  • She had been on a strict diet for months, but she finally succumbed to the temptation of chocolate cake.
  • He knew smoking was harmful, but he succumbed to peer pressure and started anyway.
  • The negotiators held firm for weeks, but eventually succumbed to the other side's demands.
  • Despite his fear, he almost succumbed to the urge to run away.

In all these examples, notice the pattern: there was a fight, and the fight was lost.

2. To die as a result of an illness or injury

This is a more formal and serious use. It means someone was fighting a disease or the effects of an injury, but could not survive it.

Examples:

  • He succumbed to cancer after a three-year battle.
  • The patient succumbed to his injuries at the hospital.
  • Thousands of people succumbed to the disease during the epidemic.

This usage is common in news writing, medical contexts, and formal speech. You would not use this meaning lightly or casually.

A few things make this word more precise and powerful than simpler alternatives:

It always implies prior resistance. This is the most important thing to remember. If someone happily and willingly accepts something with no struggle, you would not use "succumb." The word carries the weight of a fight that was eventually lost. Compare:

  • "She accepted the job offer." → No struggle. She just said yes.
  • "She finally succumbed to her boss's repeated requests to take the promotion." → She resisted for a while, but eventually gave in.

It almost always implies the outcome was unwanted. The person did not want to give in. They were trying not to. This makes the word carry a slightly sad or unfortunate tone.

It can apply to both physical and non-physical forces:

  • Physical: illness, injury, exhaustion, fire, a storm
  • Non-physical: temptation, fear, desire, pressure, curiosity, grief, charm

Understanding what a word is not is just as important as understanding what it is.

It is not the same as simply "failing."
Failing means you tried to do something and did not succeed. Succumbing means something overwhelmed you and overcame your resistance. The focus is different.

  • "He failed the exam." → He didn't pass.
  • "He succumbed to anxiety before the exam." → Anxiety overcame him.

It is not exactly the same as "surrendering."
Surrendering is usually a conscious, deliberate decision — a formal act of giving up. Succumbing can be more passive — something just overcomes you. You may not even fully realize it's happening.

It is not the same as "agreeing."
If you agree with someone after hearing their argument, you simply changed your mind. If you succumb to someone's pressure, you gave in despite not really wanting to — the pressure wore you down.
The Grammar Rule: Always Followed by "to"

This is important. "Succumb" is almost always followed by the word "to." You always succumb to something — to a disease, to temptation, to pressure, to fear.

  • ✅ She succumbed to exhaustion.
  • ✅ He succumbed to the illness.
  • ❌ She succumbed exhaustion. (incorrect)

"Succumb" is a formal or semi-formal word. You will see it often in news articles, literature, medical writing, and serious speech. In casual everyday conversation, people might instead say "gave in," "caved," or "couldn't resist" — these mean similar things but sound more informal. "Succumb" is the more precise, more dignified version.

To succumb = to stop resisting something stronger than you and give in to it — whether that is a temptation, a pressure, an emotion, or a fatal illness — often reluctantly, and after a period of struggle.
14325: To sue someone means to take them to a court of law and formally demand that they compensate you or fix a wrong they have done to you. It is a legal action that one person or organization initiates against another. When you sue someone, you are essentially saying to a court: "This person/company has wronged me, and I want the law to make it right."

Imagine your neighbor's dog bites you badly, and you end up with expensive hospital bills. Your neighbor refuses to help. You can sue them — meaning you go to court, present your case, and ask a judge to legally force your neighbor to pay for your medical expenses. The court then decides who is right.

That's suing in its most straightforward form.

When someone sues and someone gets sued, there are two sides:

  • The person doing the suing is called the plaintiff — the one who feels wronged and starts the case.
  • The person being sued is called the defendant — the one who has to go to court and defend themselves.

You can sue a person, a company, an organization, or even a government.

People sue for many reasons, all centered around the idea that someone caused them harm or violated their rights. Common reasons include:

  • Someone injured you physically (a car accident, a dog bite, a slip and fall on someone's unsafe property)
  • Someone broke a promise that was written in a contract (didn't deliver goods, didn't pay for services)
  • Someone damaged your reputation by spreading lies about you (this is called defamation)
  • A doctor made a serious mistake during your treatment (medical malpractice)
  • A company sold you a defective product that harmed you
  • An employer treated you unfairly based on your race, gender, religion, etc. (discrimination)
  • Someone damaged or stole your property
What Can You Get From Suing?

When you sue someone, you are typically asking for one or both of the following:

1. Money (called "damages")
This is the most common outcome. The court orders the other party to pay you a sum of money to compensate for your loss, suffering, or expenses. For example, if someone crashed into your car, you might sue for the repair costs plus any medical bills.

2. A Court Order (called an "injunction")
Sometimes you don't just want money — you want someone to stop doing something or start doing something. For example, if a factory near your home is illegally polluting the river, you might sue to get a court order that forces them to stop. The court can legally compel a behavior, not just award money.
Suing Is a Civil Matter, Not Criminal

This is an important distinction that confuses many people.

Criminal cases are brought by the government (the state or the country) against a person who broke the law. The punishment is usually a fine, imprisonment, or both. Ordinary citizens don't "sue" in criminal cases — the government prosecutes.

Civil cases — which is where "suing" happens — are brought by a private person or organization against another private person or organization. The goal is not to put someone in jail, but to get compensation or enforce rights.

So, if someone steals from you:

  • The government might prosecute them criminally (which could lead to jail time).
  • You might sue them civilly (to get your money or property back).

Both can happen at the same time, and they are entirely separate processes.

When you sue someone, you file a formal document with the court explaining your complaint. The other side is informed and gets a chance to respond. Both sides then present their evidence and arguments, and eventually a judge (or sometimes a jury) decides the outcome. If you win, the court issues a ruling in your favor. If you lose, you get nothing — and may even have to pay the other side's legal costs in some cases.

Many lawsuits never reach a full trial. The two sides often reach a settlement — a private agreement (usually involving a payment) — before a judge makes a final ruling. You will often hear phrases like "they settled out of court," which means they resolved it without a judge's final decision.

The word is very flexible:

  • She decided to sue the company for wrongful termination.
  • He was sued by his former business partner.
  • They threatened to sue if the refund wasn't issued.
  • The family sued the hospital for negligence.
  • You can sue for damages even if the amount is small — small claims court exists for that.
  • The construction company was sued over the building collapse.

Note the common pattern: sue + someone + for + reason/amount.
"She sued the driver for $50,000 in damages."

In older, formal, or literary English, "sue" can also mean to make a humble or earnest appeal — to plead or petition for something. This usage is rare today, but you may encounter it in older books or historical texts.

Examples:

  • The defeated army sued for peace. (They formally appealed for peace.)
  • He sued for mercy before the king. (He pleaded for mercy.)

This meaning shares the same spirit as the legal meaning — making a formal request — but it is not used in everyday modern speech. If you encounter it, it simply means "to earnestly appeal or petition."

To sue is to formally use the legal system to seek justice or compensation from someone who has wronged you. It is a civil (not criminal) action. The person suing wants either money, a court-enforced action, or both. A judge or jury ultimately decides the outcome, though most cases end in a settlement before that point.
14326:
To suffice means to be enough for a particular purpose or need. That is the heart of it. When something suffices, it meets the requirement — it does the job, it covers the need, it is adequate.

Think of it as a simple test: does X meet the minimum requirement? If yes, X suffices.
The Key Nuance: "Enough" — Not More, Not Less

This is critical to understand. "Suffice" sits right at the line of adequacy. It does not mean excellent, outstanding, or more than enough. It means at least enough — it clears the bar.

A single candle may suffice to light a small room. (It gives enough light — not great, but it works.) One explanation may suffice. (You do not need another — this one is adequate.) So when something suffices, you can stop searching. The need is met.

This verb works in three main patterns:

Pattern 1 — [Something] suffices:
The subject is simply "enough" on its own.

  • "This amount will suffice."
  • "A brief explanation suffices here."
  • "One copy suffices."

Pattern 2 — [Something] suffices for [a purpose or person]:
You name what it is enough for.

  • "This food will suffice for the whole group."
  • "A simple apology will not suffice for the damage caused."
  • "Two hours sufficed for the task."

Pattern 3 — [Something] suffices to [do something]:
You name what goal is accomplished.

  • "One dose suffices to relieve the pain."
  • "A few sentences sufficed to explain the problem."
The Most Common Phrase: "Suffice It to Say"

You will encounter this phrase very frequently. It means: "It is enough to say..." or "Let me just say this much..."

You use it when you do not want to go into full detail, but you want to make one key point clearly — usually because the full story would be too long, too painful, or simply unnecessary.

  • "Suffice it to say, the meeting did not go well." (= I won't give you every detail, but know this: it was bad.)
  • "I won't describe the whole ordeal — suffice it to say, it was the worst night of my life."
  • "He lied, he cheated, and — suffice it to say — we are no longer friends."

Think of this phrase as a way of saying: "This one statement captures everything you need to know."

"Suffice" is somewhat formal. In casual, everyday spoken English, people usually say "be enough" or "do" instead:

  • Casual: "Will this be enough?" / "This will do."
  • Formal: "Will this suffice?" / "This will suffice."

Both mean exactly the same thing. But "suffice" sounds more polished and considered, and is especially common in writing, professional settings, academic contexts, and careful speech.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what "suffice" does not mean:

It does not mean excellent. If something suffices, it is adequate — not necessarily great. "The meal sufficed" tells you people were fed. It says nothing about whether the food was delicious.

It does not mean emotionally satisfy. "That answer satisfied me" suggests you were pleased, even moved. "That answer sufficed" simply means it was enough — it answered the question. The emotional weight is absent.

It does not mean prove. You can say "this evidence suffices" (= there is enough of it), but the word itself is only saying the quantity or quality meets a threshold — not that a conclusion has been proven.

This is equally important, and very commonly used. When something does not suffice, it falls short — it is not enough.

  • "I'm afraid a verbal promise will not suffice. We need it in writing."
  • "Good intentions do not suffice — results matter."
  • "One day of practice will not suffice to master this skill."

The negative form often carries a tone of firm, clear rejection. The speaker is saying that whatever has been offered or done simply does not clear the bar.

In everyday life:

  • "Is there enough rice?" / "Yes, this should suffice for dinner."
  • "I only have five minutes — will that suffice to explain the issue?"

In professional or formal settings:

  • "A one-page summary will suffice; there is no need for a full report."
  • "Your signature on this form will suffice."
  • "The committee decided the available evidence did not suffice to reach a verdict."

In writing and literature:

  • "A single glance sufficed to tell her everything."
  • "No words could suffice to express his gratitude."
One Final Way to Think About It

Imagine a cup. Your need is the cup. Something suffices when it fills that cup — right to the brim, or at least enough to serve its purpose. It does not overflow (that would be more than enough). It does not leave the cup half-empty (that would not suffice). It simply meets the level.

That is "suffice" in its entirety: to meet the level of what is needed — no more is required, and no less will do.
14327:
Sufficient means enough to meet a need or purpose — not too little, and not necessarily more than needed. Just the right amount to satisfy a requirement.

Think of it like filling a bucket that needs to be full to water a garden. If you pour in exactly enough water to fill it, that water is sufficient. If you pour in less, it's not sufficient. If you pour in extra, well, that's more than sufficient — but the point is, sufficient simply means the need is met.
The Key Insight: Sufficient Is Always Relative to a Goal

This is the most important thing to understand: sufficient never stands alone in meaning. It always answers the question, "Enough for what?"

The same amount can be sufficient in one situation and completely insufficient in another.

  • One candle may be sufficient to light a small room, but not sufficient to light a stadium.
  • Three hours of sleep might be sufficient for a short nap, but not sufficient for a full night's rest.
  • A pinch of salt may be sufficient for a single egg, but not sufficient for a large pot of pasta.

The word is always pointing at a specific standard or purpose. Once that purpose is met, the thing qualifies as sufficient.

Understanding a word also means knowing what it doesn't mean.

Sufficient ≠ Plentiful or Abundant
Sufficient doesn't suggest that there's a lot of something. It only says there's enough. If you have just barely enough money to pay a bill, that money is sufficient — even if it leaves you with nothing left over.

Sufficient ≠ Perfect or Ideal
Something can be sufficient without being great or ideal. A simple meal can be sufficient to keep you from being hungry. It doesn't have to be a feast.

Sufficient ≠ More Than Enough
Words like ample, abundant, or plentiful go further — they mean more than what's needed. Sufficient stays right at the line of "just enough."

The direct opposite of sufficient is insufficient, which means not enough — falling short of what is needed.

  • There was insufficient evidence to prove he was guilty. (Not enough evidence.)
  • She had insufficient time to finish the exam. (Not enough time.)

"Sufficient" is slightly more formal than its close cousin "enough." In everyday speech, people usually say enough. In writing, legal language, academic work, science, and professional settings, sufficient is very common.

Casual: "Do we have enough food for the party?"
Formal: "The provisions should be sufficient for all attendees."

Both sentences mean the same thing. The difference is just the level of formality.
How It Behaves in a Sentence

As an adjective, "sufficient" usually appears in two positions:

Before a noun:

  • "We need sufficient time to complete the project."
  • "She gave sufficient reasons for her decision."

After a linking verb (like "is," "was," "seems"):

  • "The evidence is sufficient."
  • "One coat of paint was sufficient."
  • "Your explanation seems sufficient."

It is also commonly followed by "to + verb" or "for + noun" to name the purpose:

  • "Is this rope strong enough?" → "Is this rope sufficient to hold the weight?"
  • "There is sufficient funding for the research."
  • "She had sufficient skill to pass the test."

Law:
"The prosecution did not present sufficient evidence to secure a conviction."
→ The evidence didn't meet the legal standard required. Not enough.

Science:
"The temperature was sufficient to cause the chemical reaction."
→ The temperature reached the threshold needed to trigger the reaction.

Daily Life:
"I don't think I have sufficient cash on me — can I pay by card?"
→ The speaker's cash might not cover the cost.

Work:
"Your qualifications are sufficient for this role."
→ You meet the requirements. You qualify.

Instructions:
"Add water until the mixture is of sufficient consistency."
→ Keep adding water until the mixture reaches the right thickness.

In logic and reasoning, you'll often see the phrase "sufficient condition." This means: if this thing is true or present, it guarantees a result.

For example: "Being over 18 is a sufficient condition to vote in many countries." If you're over 18, that alone is enough — you qualify. You don't need anything else on top of that.

This is a precise, logical use of the word and you'll see it often in academic or analytical writing.

Sufficient = Enough to meet a specific need or purpose — no more is required, and nothing is lacking.

It's a word about meeting a threshold. It's context-sensitive, slightly formal, and always implies a standard being measured against. When something is sufficient, the job is done — the requirement is satisfied.
14328:
To suffocate means to die, or to nearly die, because of a lack of air — or to cause someone else to die that way.

Think of it this way: your body needs air (specifically, oxygen) every single moment to stay alive. When something blocks that air — whether it's smoke, water, a tight space, or something covering your face — your body starts to shut down. That experience, or the act of causing it, is what "suffocate" describes.
The Two Basic Ways It Is Used

1. Without causing it to someone (you yourself are the one struggling)

Here, the subject is the person or thing that is running out of air.

"The man was trapped in the airtight room and began to suffocate."
"Several miners suffocated when the tunnel collapsed and cut off the air supply."
"A fish out of water will suffocate."

In these sentences, nobody is doing anything to these people or creatures — the circumstances themselves are cutting off their air.

2. Causing it to happen to someone else

Here, one person or thing is actively depriving another of air.

"The thick smoke suffocated the people trapped on the upper floors."
"He suffocated the candle flame by placing a glass over it."

In these sentences, something external is the cause — it is acting upon the victim and taking away their air.

This is important. Suffocate does not always mean someone actually dies. It is frequently used to describe the feeling or process of struggling to breathe — even when the person survives.

"She pulled her scarf too tight and felt like she was suffocating."
"The air in the crowded subway was so stale that passengers were suffocating."

In these cases, they are not dead — they are gasping, struggling, and desperate for fresh air. The word captures that distressing experience perfectly.

This is where "suffocate" becomes truly powerful in the English language. People use it constantly to describe emotional, mental, or social situations that feel like being deprived of air — situations where you feel trapped, controlled, overwhelmed, or unable to express yourself freely.

Just as a lack of air makes the body desperate and unable to function, a lack of freedom, space, or choice can make the mind and spirit feel the same way.

"She felt suffocated in her marriage because her partner controlled every little thing she did."
"Growing up in a very strict household, he felt suffocated and longed for independence."
"The new employee was suffocating under the enormous pressure of impossible deadlines."
"Years of heavy taxation suffocated small businesses in the region."
"His over-protective parenting was suffocating his child's natural curiosity."

Notice how in all these examples, nobody is literally losing oxygen — but the feeling is the same: trapped, helpless, unable to breathe or move freely. This figurative use is extremely common and natural in everyday English.
Suffocate as a Description of Atmosphere or Environment

You will often see "suffocating" (the adjective form of the verb) used to describe places, heat, or atmospheres that feel so heavy, hot, or stifling that being in them feels physically uncomfortable — like the air itself is too thick.

"The July heat was suffocating — stepping outside felt like walking into a wall of hot, wet air."
"The room was small, windowless, and suffocating."
"The tension between the two rivals created a suffocating atmosphere in the office."
Suffocate vs. Choke vs. Drown — What's the Difference?

These words are neighbours, so it's worth knowing how they differ.

  • Suffocate = losing air in any situation — smoke, sealed spaces, something covering the face, lack of oxygen at high altitude, etc.
  • Choke = specifically, something is blocking the throat or airway (usually food, an object, or hands around the neck). Choking is one way someone can suffocate, but suffocating is the broader word.
  • Drown = specifically losing air because of water filling the lungs.

So: you can drown in a river and choke on a piece of meat — and in both cases, you are technically suffocating, because the end result is the same: no air reaches the lungs.

FormExample
suffocate (base)"People can suffocate in airtight spaces."
suffocates"Pollution suffocates marine life."
suffocated"Three people suffocated in the fire."
suffocating (ongoing action or adjective)"The suffocating heat made it hard to think."
suffocation (the noun)"The cause of death was suffocation."

To suffocate means to be deprived of the air needed to survive — causing death or severe distress — whether physically (from smoke, sealed spaces, or obstruction) or figuratively (from emotional control, pressure, or restriction that makes life feel unbearable).
14329:
Suffrage means the right to vote — specifically, the legal right of a citizen to participate in choosing their government or leaders through voting in elections.

Notice this carefully: suffrage is not the act of voting. It is the right to vote. This is an important distinction. A person might have the right to vote but choose not to go to the polls on election day. They still have suffrage. But if the law prevents them from voting at all — because of their gender, race, wealth, or any other reason — then they lack suffrage. The word is about whether you are permitted and entitled to vote, not whether you actually did.

Think of suffrage as a kind of permission granted by society and law. For most of human history, this permission was extremely limited. Only certain people — usually wealthy men who owned land — were considered worthy of having a say in governance. Everyone else was excluded. The story of suffrage, therefore, is the story of humanity slowly expanding this circle of permission to include more and more people.

This is exactly why you will most often encounter the word in two famous phrases:

Women's suffrage refers to the movement — and its ultimate success — to grant women the legal right to vote. For centuries, women were excluded from elections entirely. In the United States, women gained the right to vote in 1920 through the 19th Amendment. In the United Kingdom, women over 30 gained it in 1918, and equal voting rights with men came in 1928. The women (and men) who fought for this cause were called suffragists or, more militantly, suffragettes.

Universal suffrage means that all adult citizens of a country have the right to vote, without restriction based on gender, race, religion, wealth, or social class. This is the standard that most modern democracies aim for today. The word "universal" here simply means the right extends to everyone, universally. In practice, most countries still exclude non-citizens, people below a certain age (usually 18), and in some places, imprisoned individuals — but the core ideal of universal suffrage is that no law unfairly singles out a group and strips them of their vote.

In older texts and in formal or religious writing, suffrage can also mean a vote itself — the actual ballot or expression of choice cast by a person. So instead of saying "he cast his vote in favour of the proposal," an older or more formal writer might say "he gave his suffrage to the proposal." This usage is rare today but worth knowing, especially if you read historical documents or classical literature.

In Christian religious tradition (particularly in Anglican and Catholic churches), the word "suffrages" is also used for short intercessory prayers — prayers offered on behalf of others. This is a very specialized meaning confined to religious contexts and is largely separate from the political meaning the word carries in everyday modern usage.
Why the Word Carries Such Weight

Suffrage is not a neutral, clinical word. It carries enormous moral and historical weight because the denial of suffrage was one of the most powerful tools of oppression in history. When a government told women, or Black citizens, or the poor that they had no right to vote, it was effectively telling them: your opinions about your own governance do not count. You are not full members of this society. This is why winning suffrage — gaining the right to vote — was understood as far more than a bureaucratic change. It was a profound recognition of a group's full humanity and citizenship.

SenseMeaning

In short: suffrage = the right to vote. When a group is said to have won suffrage, they have won the legal recognition that they are entitled to participate in democracy. When suffrage is denied, a group is locked out of having any formal voice in how their society is governed. It is one of the most fundamental concepts in democracy and political history.
